item.title: Jozankei Onsen — Guide
item.description: Jozankei Onsen, set in a beautiful forested river valley only about an hour southwest of central Sapporo, is the city’s most convenient and popular hot-spring (onsen) resort. Nestled along the Toyohira River within the Shikotsu-Toya National Park, this atmospheric spa town has been welcoming bathers since the 1860s and offers a relaxing retreat of hot-spring ryokan and hotels, day-use baths, free public foot baths (ashiyu) and hand baths dotted around town.

item.title: Osaka Autumn Foliage: Minoo Falls and the Momiji Trail — Guide
item.description: For autumn colour, Osakans head north to Minoo (Mino-o), a wooded valley on the edge of the city that turns brilliant with maples each November. A gentle, paved riverside trail runs about three kilometres up the gorge from Minoo Station to the Minoo Waterfall, a 33-metre fall framed by fiery leaves at the head of the valley — one of the most rewarding easy walks in the Osaka area. Along the way, shops sell the local speciality of momiji tempura, whole maple leaves battered and deep-fried into a sweet, crisp snack.

item.title: Rikugien Garden — Guide
item.description: Rikugien, in Tokyo’s Bunkyo ward, is widely regarded as one of the city’s most beautiful traditional Japanese gardens. Completed in 1702, this Edo-period ‘strolling garden’ was designed to recreate in miniature 88 scenes from classical Japanese and Chinese poetry, laid out around a large central pond with small islands, wooded hills, winding paths, stone bridges and elegant teahouses. A leisurely circuit reveals ever-changing views, and you can pause at a teahouse for matcha and a sweet overlooking the water.

item.title: Tanzan Shrine: The Wooden Pagoda in the Autumn Hills — Guide
item.description: Tanzan Shrine, tucked into the wooded mountains south of Sakurai, is one of Nara’s most beautiful hidden gems, dedicated to Fujiwara no Kamatari, founder of the mighty Fujiwara clan, whose plot to reform the state was supposedly hatched on this mountain. Its treasure is unique: a graceful vermilion thirteen-story wooden pagoda, the only one of its kind surviving anywhere in the world, rising in tiers among the trees. The shrine is above all an autumn destination, when some 3,000 maple trees set the mountainside ablaze in reds and golds around the pagoda, one of the finest foliage sights in the Kansai region.

item.title: Oirase Stream: Aomori's Most Beautiful Forest Walk — Guide
item.description: The Oirase Stream is a designated National Scenic Treasure — 14 km of pristine forest gorge threaded by a rushing mountain stream and dotted with named waterfalls. The trail between Yakeyama and Nenokuchi is one of Japan’s most celebrated nature walks, reaching its peak in late-October foliage. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Towada-Hachimantai NP, Aomori Hours Trail always open (daylight best) Admission Free Time needed 2–4 hours (walk sections) Best time Late Oct–early Nov (autumn); fresh green in June What to See The Choshi Otaki and Kumoi falls among 14 named cascades.

item.title: Hokkaido Autumn Foliage Guide: Best Spots & Time (Sep–Oct)
item.description: Autumn comes first to Hokkaido — Japan’s earliest foliage flames into life on the high peaks in September, weeks ahead of the mainland, before sweeping down to the lakes, valleys and city parks through October. The island’s huge wild landscapes make for spectacular koyo: golden birch and larch, crimson maples and mountain ash against volcanic peaks and mirror-still caldera lakes. From the alpine slopes of Daisetsuzan to the gorges of Sounkyo and the onsen valley of Jozankei, Hokkaido’s autumn is a quieter, wilder counterpoint to Kyoto’s crowds.

item.title: Minoo Park Guide: Waterfall, Autumn Leaves & Fried Maple Leaves
item.description: Just half an hour from central Osaka, Minoo Park (Mino-o) is the city’s favourite nature escape — a forested river valley climbing gently to the lovely 33-metre Minoo Waterfall. The paved riverside trail is easy enough for almost anyone, lined with old tea houses and shops, and in November the maples turn the whole gorge brilliant red and gold. It’s also famous for a uniquely Osaka snack: momiji tempura, real maple leaves battered and deep-fried into a sweet, crispy treat.

item.title: Mount Takao Guide: Tokyo's Best Day Hike with Mt. Fuji Views
item.description: Less than an hour from the neon of Shinjuku, a forested 599-metre mountain rises out of Tokyo’s western suburbs and offers, on a clear day, a view of Mount Fuji floating on the horizon. Mount Takao (Takao-san) is the most-climbed mountain in the world — over three million people a year — and for good reason: it’s astonishingly accessible, suits every fitness level from sneaker-wearing tourists to serious hikers, holds a thousand-year-old mountain temple, and rewards you at the bottom with a beer garden.

item.title: Okutama Guide: Tokyo's Wild Mountain Frontier
item.description: Most people are astonished to learn that Tokyo — the word that means glass towers and 37 million people — also contains genuine mountain wilderness. Travel two hours west of Shinjuku and the metropolis gives way entirely to steep forested valleys, crystal-clear rivers, a turquoise reservoir, and limestone caves: this is Okutama, the mountainous far-western edge of Tokyo Prefecture, part of the Chichibu-Tama-Kai National Park. Here you can kayak on a mountain lake, walk through a gorge, descend into a cave, soak in a hot spring, and stand among some of the Kanto region’s finest autumn colour — all without leaving Tokyo.

item.title: Yoro Valley Guide: Onsen, Autumn Leaves & Access
item.description: Tucked into the green heart of the Boso Peninsula, Yoro Valley (Yorokeikoku) is Chiba’s premier nature escape — a winding river gorge of clear pools, waterfalls and forested ridges that erupts into brilliant colour each autumn. It’s one of the latest-colouring autumn-leaf spots near Tokyo (late November to early December), and its riverside onsen ryokan let you soak among the foliage. Walking trails lead to the photogenic Awamata Falls and a curious old road tunnel, while the rural Kominato and Isumi railways make getting there half the fun.

item.title: Miyagi Nature: Naruko Gorge Autumn Leaves, Sanriku Coast & Tohoku Wilderness
item.description: Miyagi Prefecture Nature and Outdoor Guide for International Visitors Miyagi Prefecture, anchored by the modern city of Sendai in Japan’s Tohoku region, offers extraordinary natural diversity—from one of Japan’s most celebrated gorges to a rugged Pacific coastline shaped by both geological forces and recent history. This guide reveals the prefecture’s finest outdoor experiences for international visitors seeking authentic encounters with Japanese nature and meaningful cultural landscapes. 1. Naruko Gorge (鳴子峡): Tohoku’s Autumn Masterpiece Naruko Gorge ranks among Japan’s most spectacular autumn destinations, though it remains refreshingly uncrowded compared to Kyoto’s famous sites.
